description: UT thickness surveys of water tanks, steel pipe, penstocks and plant steelwork for US utilities before rehabilitation. Crews travel to you. Get a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing for Water and Wastewater Utilities
html:
Ultrasonic testing for water and wastewater utilities in the United States is mostly thickness work: measuring how much steel remains in welded storage tanks, steel pipe, penstocks, pump station headers and treatment plant steelwork before the utility spends money on coating or rehabilitation. Atlantis mobilizes SNT-TC-1A qualified technicians to your tank site, pump station or plant for the agreed scope and returns a gridded thickness report that your engineer can design from. To scope a survey, request a UT thickness inspection quote.

What utilities ask ultrasonic testing to answer

A water utility rarely asks for ultrasonic testing because of a suspected crack. It asks because a steel asset has been in service for decades under a coating that is failing, and someone has to decide whether the steel is worth recoating, needs repair, or should be replaced. The deliverable that supports that decision is a map of remaining wall thickness, tied to a known baseline, with the thinnest locations highlighted and the survey method stated.

That is where ultrasonic thickness testing earns its place. It reads wall thickness from one side, it works on steel of almost any age, and it gives numbers a design engineer can use. It does not find tight surface cracks reliably, so weld toes and repairs are examined by the MT page for water utilities or the PT page where those methods fit.

Welded steel storage tanks and standpipes

AWWA D100 is the standard for welded carbon steel tanks for water storage, and AWWA D101 covers inspecting and repairing steel water tanks, standpipes, reservoirs and elevated tanks. Ground storage tanks, standpipes and elevated tanks each concentrate corrosion in different places. The waterline zone, the roof underside and its support steel, the floor and the shell-to-floor junction take most of the attack, and in cold regions ice can damage the shell near the waterline.

Elevated tanks add a bowl, a riser pipe or tubular column, and leg bracing. We survey shell courses on a grid, check the roof plate where access allows, and take readings on riser and column walls. The tank must be taken out of service and drained for interior floor and underside readings; we do not offer diver or underwater survey work, and a tank that stays in service is surveyed from the exterior and from accessible interior areas only. Our broader tank inspection page explains how the full condition assessment is organized.

Steel water pipe, large-diameter mains and penstocks

AWWA C200 covers steel water pipe 6 inches and larger, and AWWA Manual M11 is the design and installation guide that engineers use with it. Large-diameter steel mains, transmission lines and penstocks are typically welded or have field-welded joints, and they are lined with cement mortar or another lining and coated outside. The lining and the exterior coating are barriers that must be addressed before a clean reading is possible.

Where pipe is exposed in a vault, a river crossing, an aerial crossing or an excavated section, we take thickness on a defined grid around the circumference and along the length, and we examine field weld areas where the owner identifies them. From the outside, mortar coating or tape wrap has to be removed at the test location. From the inside, entry is under your confined space program, and the lining condition changes what the gauge sees. The job-specific description for piping is on the ultrasonic pipe thickness testing page.

We do not run any in-line inspection tool through a main. Where a utility wants a screening of a long line, that is a different service, and our work begins at the excavation, vault or access point the utility opens.

Pump stations and treatment plant steelwork

Pump station discharge headers, suction manifolds, surge vessels and interconnecting piping see pulsation and, in wastewater service, hydrogen sulfide. In a treatment plant, clarifier mechanisms, center columns and walkway steelwork, digester tanks and covers, and process piping are all thickness survey candidates. Digester gas piping and covers carry an added hazard of flammable and toxic gas, and entry or hot work there follows the plant's permit system.

Sewer force mains and dewatering piping made of steel are surveyed at accessible points, such as pump station piping, valve vaults and air-release assemblies, where corrosion from sulfide is common. For flat structural steel and equipment bases, we use the same grid method and record the surface condition at each point, because pitted surfaces influence the reading.

Technique details for water infrastructure

  • Through coating. Utility steel is often coated. A reading through an intact coating is acceptable only when the technique has been verified on that coating and the report says what was measured. Otherwise coating is removed at each test location by the owner's contractor.
  • Lead and hazardous coatings. Older tanks may carry lead-based paint. Disturbing it falls under OSHA's lead rules and the owner's abatement plan, and we ask for that information before mobilizing.
  • Calibration. Instruments are calibrated on steel blocks bracketing the expected thickness, following ASME Section V Article 5 and ASTM E797 for manual contact thickness measurement. Block and instrument serial numbers go on the report.
  • Pitting. Wide-area grids can miss isolated pits. Where pitting is visible, the technician adds readings around each pit and records the lowest reading with a sketch.
  • Temperature and moisture. Wet, cold or sun-heated steel affects couplant choice. Readings on water-cooled surfaces and sun-baked roof plates are handled with the proper couplant and noted.
  • Repeatability. Grid origin, spacing and point numbering are drawn on the sketch, so a later survey can repeat the same points and show wall loss over time.

Codes, regulators and who decides acceptance

The Safe Drinking Water Act sets the broader framework for public water systems, with state drinking water programs enforcing it. Coating and lining materials that touch drinking water are normally required to meet NSF/ANSI 61, which is the coating contractor's concern rather than ours. For steel tank and pipe condition, the utility's engineer applies AWWA D100, AWWA D101, AWWA C200 and AWWA Manual M11 as appropriate, and ASME Section V sets the ultrasonic method. Atlantis reports thickness against the nominal and minimum values the utility's engineer provides. We do not calculate remaining life, set inspection intervals or decide fitness for service; the engineer of record decides repair, recoating or replacement.

When ultrasonic testing is not the right choice

Ultrasonic thickness testing is a poor tool for tight surface cracks in welds, and for those you want magnetic particle or penetrant examination. It is also a poor tool for a flat coating-disbond question, a leak-location question or a structural capacity calculation. It cannot see a void behind cement mortar lining from the outside, and it cannot give a pass or fail on joint integrity of a gasketed bell-and-spigot joint. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US; where code calls for it, the utility hires a licensed contractor.

What the report contains

ItemWhat you receive
Asset identificationTank, pipe or equipment ID, location, nominal thickness and design drawings referenced

What to send for a quote

  • Asset list: tanks, standpipes, pipe segments, headers, equipment with IDs and drawings
  • Diameter, plate or wall thickness, material, and design standard such as AWWA D100 or C200
  • Prior survey data or original plate maps for a repeatable grid
  • Coating type and condition, any lead or hazardous coating, and who removes coating at test points
  • Whether the asset will be out of service, drained and cleaned
  • Access: scaffolding, lifts, rope access arranged by the utility, vault entry details
  • Confined space entry permit process and rescue plan
  • Site address, background check or badge requirements for critical infrastructure

Planning around operations

Utilities schedule tank work in seasons of low demand, and pipe work around main shutdown windows set by operations. Entry into drained tanks, vaults and wet wells follows 29 CFR 1910.146 or, for construction activity, the construction confined space rules in 29 CFR 1926, together with the utility's own permit program. Many sites also require background checks or escort. Atlantis technicians travel to your site with their own gauges, blocks and couplant, and the schedule is set once the utility confirms access and the date the asset will be available.

Training in-house utility staff

Some utilities want a maintenance or asset management team that can take routine thickness readings. UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training follow SNT-TC-1A, and the ultrasonic testing simulator provides practice before live equipment. Your utility certifies its own personnel under a written practice, and written practice development helps set that up. Our procedure development service writes the thickness procedure your engineer can review, and the guide to ASME Section V Article 5 explains the code basis. The national page is ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Can you measure steel thickness on a water tank without draining it?
faq.a: Shell and roof areas reachable from the outside can be measured with the tank in service. Floor and interior readings need the tank drained and cleaned. We do not provide diver or underwater work, so submerged areas are outside our scope.

faq.q: Do you measure through the coating on a water tank or pipe?
faq.a: Sometimes. A reading through an intact coating is acceptable only when the technique is verified on that coating and the report states what was measured. Otherwise the owner's contractor removes the coating at each test point.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a tank thickness survey?
faq.a: Send tank type, dimensions, plate thickness and material, prior survey data, coating information including lead, access arrangements, whether it will be drained, entry permit steps and the site address with any security requirements.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be done on steel pipe lined with cement mortar?
faq.a: From the outside on exposed steel, yes, once exterior coating is removed. From the inside, the lining affects the reading and the report must state what was measured. The technician cannot judge lining condition by ultrasonic thickness alone.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the thickness readings?
faq.a: The utility's engineer of record sets the minimum acceptable thickness under AWWA standards and decides on recoating, repair or replacement. Atlantis reports readings against the nominal and minimum values supplied and flags locations below them.

faq.q: Do you run inspection tools through water mains?
faq.a: No. We do not run in-line tools. We survey the pipe at excavations, vaults, crossings and access points the utility opens, measuring exposed steel and examining welds where the engineer identifies them.

faq.q: Are your technicians allowed in confined spaces such as wet wells and tanks?
faq.a: Technicians enter only under the utility's confined space permit program, following 29 CFR 1910.146 or the construction confined space rules, with atmospheric testing and rescue arrangements provided or approved by the utility.

We do not remove coatings. If a tank may carry lead paint, tell us at quotation. The owner's coating or abatement contractor prepares test points under its own lead program, and our technicians follow site rules on protective equipment.

faq.q: Is this a fitness-for-service or remaining life assessment?
faq.a: No. We provide thickness data and a report. Remaining life, intervals and fitness for service are calculated by the utility's engineer using our readings, and we do not make those calculations.
